items.title: Someone Has Made the Dreamcast Play Nintendo 64 Cartridges, Because Apparently It Can
items.content:
Sega Dreamcast artwork, supplied by the author.

The Sega Dreamcast was capable of some remarkable things. It could connect to the internet, had a memory card with its own tiny screen, and played host to some of Sega's most inventive games. What it couldn't do, for fairly obvious reasons, was play Nintendo 64 cartridges. Apparently, though, nobody told a hardware enthusiast known as Throaty Mumbo.

His project, Dreamcart , allows a Dreamcast to read physical N64 cartridges through a homemade adapter connected to the console's controller port. And because apparently one unlikely combination wasn't enough, he's also built readers for Super Nintendo and Mega Drive cartridges. None of this is a ready-made accessory you can buy and plug in, but the fact that it works at all is insane, and amazing.

In the project's documentation, Throaty Mumbo explains that using original cartridges makes it possible to access their existing save data. He also offers a simpler reason for pursuing the idea: "using actual cartridges is cooler." I think that probably tells you everything you need to know about the spirit of the project.

The Dreamcart 64 prototype with a physical Super Mario 64 cartridge. A Cartridge Reader in the Controller Port

Nintendo's N64 and Sega's Dreamcast were contemporary rivals, but they approached game storage rather differently. Nintendo stuck with cartridges, while Sega's final console used GD-ROM discs. Dreamcart bridges that gap with a custom cartridge reader built around an RP2350B microcontroller, connected to the Dreamcast through its Maple Bus, the interface normally used by controllers and accessories.

A look inside the N64 cartridge reader, showing the microcontroller and wiring. The reader retrieves data from the cartridge, while software on the Dreamcast attempts to run the game. For N64 titles, this involves dynamic recompilation: translating the original game's processor instructions into something the Dreamcast can execute as it runs, rather than simply pretending that the two consoles contain the same hardware. It's an ambitious undertaking for a machine that wasn't designed with Nintendo's cartridges, processor or graphics hardware in mind.

An original Donkey Kong Country cartridge being inserted into the Super Dreamcart reader. There's even a system for caching translated code, using the reader's onboard storage or an optional SD card to help with subsequent launches. On the Dreamcast itself, a Dreamcart 64 interface detects the connected reader and attempts to identify the inserted cartridge. Sometimes the result is less elegant than it sounds, with a game failing to appear or showing a garbled name until the cartridge is reinserted. That feels appropriately authentic for anyone who's ever had to persuade old hardware to cooperate.

The Dreamcast’s homebrew loader, used during the developer’s demonstrations. Mario Kart on a Sega Console!

So what actually runs? Throaty Mumbo maintains a compatibility list based on the cartridges he owns and has tested. It includes Super Mario 64 , Mario Kart 64 , Kirby 64 , Rayman 2 , Cruis'n USA and Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2 . Perhaps the most unexpected entry is Elmo's Number Journey , which is surely not a game Sega's engineers ever expected to see running on their console.

The Dreamcart prototype under test, with Super Mario 64 visible on the nearby screen. The results aren't universally successful though. Pokémon Stadium 2 is listed as barely supported, while Donkey Kong 64 doesn't work. And a game appearing on the supported list doesn't necessarily mean perfect performance throughout. This is still experimental software, not a replacement for an N64 or a polished modern emulator.

The save system is super clever, too. Where a game stores progress directly on its cartridge, Dreamcart can access that data. For titles that used Nintendo's separate Controller Pak, the Dreamcast's own Visual Memory Unit can provide the equivalent storage instead. There are…

items.title: Scheduling the removal of the kube-proxy IPVS backend
items.content:
The ipvs backend for kube-proxy was an experiment in providing a

service proxy implementation with better performance than the

iptables backend. While it succeeded in that goal, the kernel IPVS

API has turned out to be a bad match for the Kubernetes Services API,

and the ipvs backend was never able to implement all of the edge

cases of Kubernetes Service functionality correctly.

In Kubernetes 1.29, the project introduced the nftables backend for

kube-proxy, which became GA in 1.33. Part of the plan behind adding

the nftables backend was the idea that it would eventually replace

both the iptables and ipvs backends. Because the ipvs backend in

particular is complex, not 100% feature complete, and architecturally

quite different from the other two backends (and thus more work to

maintain), Kubernetes SIG Network decided to officially deprecate it

as of Kubernetes 1.35 . Although it currently remains available in

kube-proxy (with a warning about its deprecation), we (Kubernetes SIG

Network) now plan to remove it in Kubernetes 1.40. All ipvs users

should therefore be planning to migrate to either the nftables or

The ipvs backend was originally designed to fix two different kinds

of performance problems in the iptables backend:

First, iptables had problems with data plane latency (the speed

at which clients could establish new connections to services),

because kube-proxy would write a separate iptables rule to match

each service IP, so every new connection would need to be matched

against a long series of rules that was O(n) in the number of

Second, it had an even larger problem with control plane latency

(the speed at which kube-proxy could process changes to services and

endpoints and update the data plane rules), because kube-proxy would

rewrite the entire iptables ruleset every time any service or

endpoint changed. While the list of rules itself was only O(n)

in the total number of endpoints, the amount of time, RAM, and CPU

that it took to process the updated ruleset grew faster than that.

In very large clusters, kube-proxy would use 100% of one CPU all the

time just to process iptables updates. (In fact, the control plane

scaling problem was bad enough that for most users it was not even

possible to grow the cluster to the size where the data plane

The ipvs backend solved both of these scaling problems. The data

plane problem was solved mostly automatically, because the kernel IPVS

subsystem uses hash tables rather than linear lookup. The

control-plane problem was solved by not rewriting the entire

ruleset on every update. (The kernel IPVS API doesn’t have a way of

doing batch updates anyway, so this was essentially forced.)

Almost from the start, the ipvs backend also had problems.

The first version didn’t have 100% compatibility with the iptables

backend, but it was assumed that this would be fixed over time.

Unfortunately, the original authors moved on to other things outside

the Kubernetes ecosystem (as inevitably sometimes happens in open

source), and it took a while to find new people interested in

Meanwhile, as people began using the ipvs backend in larger and

larger clusters, its own scaling problems started to emerge. In

particular, the lack of batch update operations in the IPVS API meant

that while the ipvs backend was faster than iptables when making a

few small changes, it was potentially slower when making a large

number of changes at once. And because the IPVS API is fairly limited

in what it can do, kube-proxy's ipvs backend needed to fall back to

using iptables to implement various features of Kubernetes Services

beyond basic "load balancing", making it run into some of the same

scaling problems the iptables backend has. While the ipvs backend

tried to mitigate this by using ipset for some of its rules, this

again ran into the problem of not having a batch update API.

items.title: 글 쌌다 지웠다 하는 뷩쉰은 봐라
items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

개별 이미지들의 위치 변경, 삭제, 별칭 추가, 폴더명 변경을 할 수 있습니다

items.title: Improving the Wii U's Wii Mode
items.content:
One feature of the Wii U is the backwards compatibility with Wii games through Wii Mode, often referred to as vWii. In theory, this is a really nice way to enjoy Wii games on a modern TV, since the Wii U has HDMI output. Unfortunately, Wii Mode does not look great. Ironically, the output of an original Wii can look better.

The two most prominent issues are the force-cropped output and color bleed issues.

Scaled up image of the chroma bleed issue in Super Mario Sunshine and The Legend of Zelda: Skyward Sword.

You can see the green tint on the left side of the characters. (Image credit: Rulumi)

Reports of these issues go back to 2013 [1] , shortly after the Wii U was released, but a fix was never provided.

In this blog post we'll take a closer look at the technical architecture of Wii Mode graphics, how two simple typos in the firmware caused these issues, and what modern AMD GPUs have in common with the Wii U.

So who can we blame for these issues? One candidate is the DMCU. To get a quick overview of the DMCU, I'm quoting fail0verflow's description from their 2014 Wii U blog post [2] :

You may have noticed that good old VI (the display controller / Video Interface of ye olde GameCube and Wii) is gone. Huh? How does that work? Turns out they’re emulating that in software and translating its configuration to the R7xx’s CRTC registers. But where does this emulation software run? Sneaky: they added a special microcontroller to the Latte just for this purpose. The DMCU is a 68HC11 compatible 8-bit CPU whose sole purpose is to perform VI emulation. It has a frontend hardware shim that looks like VI to the Wii software, and behind the scenes it translates those registers to the Radeon’s, including upscaling configuration. cafe2wii loads the DMCU’s firmware (the DMCU doesn’t seem to be active in Wii U mode). It has its own dedicated RAM and access to both the faux-VI back side and the Radeon’s register area. [...]

To get to the bottom of these issues, I decided to reverse-engineer the firmware of the DMCU. The DMCU firmware is located in the Wii U's storage and is loaded into the DMCU's RAM before launching cafe2wii. Unfortunately, my favorite reverse-engineering tool Ghidra does not support the HC11, so in 2024 I ended up writing my own processor specification for it [3] . Luckily, Ghidra already supported the HCS08 and HCS12, which I could base my specification on.

I then spent several days reverse-engineering the DMCU firmware. The firmware itself is relatively straightforward. The DMCU has an interface to access the 32-bit registers of the display controller. The faux-VI hardware shim triggers interrupts in the DMCU firmware, which then configures the display controller accordingly.

Reverse engineering the DMCU quickly reveals the reason for the cropped image. The DMCU configures the display controller's viewport to simulate overscan. This crops off up to 16 pixels, which does not look great in several titles. Luckily, this is an easy fix; I can simply patch the bytes of the firmware directly to change the values written to the viewport registers.

What fail0verflow didn't know at the time, or at least didn't mention, is that the DMCU is not a Wii U-specific microcontroller, but is found in other AMD GPUs too. A patch submitted by an AMD employee in 2018 to the amd-gfx mailing list [4] mentions the following:

DMCU (Display Microcontroller Unit) is a GPU chip involved in eDP features like Adaptive Backlight Modulation and Panel Self Refresh.

At least now we know what DMCU stands for. Could this really be the same chip design as used by the Wii U? The linux-firmware repository has several DMCU binary blobs for different GPUs [5] . After downloading raven_dmcu.bin and navi12_dmcu.bin , I wrote a quick tool to parse the headers of the firmware blobs and extract the part that actually gets loaded into ERAM [6] .

After loading the AMD Raven and Navi 12 DMCU firmware into Ghidra, I was able to confirm that the newer AMD GPUs…

items.title: Software is breaking down at a systemic level, by Jimmy Breck-McKye
items.content:
Software hasn’t been working too well lately, has it?

This weekend we saw the double-whammy of a 2 day global Microsoft outage, then an FAA ground-stop that halted all flights in the United States.

Can you believe it’s only been four weeks since the PHP2Shell vulnerability? A critical exploit in PHP, powering an estimated 70% of the world’s websites, with sites taken completely offline as engineers frantically patched their systems.

And then there was the eMudhra fiasco , where thousands of SSL certificates - the way we secure HTTPS websites and internet traffic - were compromised by a private key so weak, it was almost comical.

It’s like 2026 has been a year of hacks, outages, vulnerabilities and IT panics. What exactly is going on here?

You might be tempted to blame AI, and you wouldn’t be completely wrong. Artificial intelligence models are definitely a part of this. Even if companies like Microsoft don’t divulge whether broken systems were built with AI, we do know that hackers and researchers can now use AI technology to find complicated exploits in a matter of hours.

I work with AI heavily in my job. It’s tremendously powerful. It’s also corrosive if used unwisely.

But AI is both a cause and a symptom of the problem here. What we are seeing is software breaking down at a systemic level. This problem is insidious because it is not only the software itself that is broken, but the entire way we’ve come to build it.

What does it mean for a failure to be systemic?

Look at the recent crises in software reliability and you’ll notice they don’t share immediate causes - that we know of - yet they look uncannily similar to each other.

The Microsoft outage likely emerged from a network configuration failure that stopped MS datacenters communicating with each other. Exactly what happened next remains confidential, but it seems to have triggered a cascading failure where no service could be restored into a valid state long enough to bear traffic.

Reddit and Bluesky speculated that even MSFT engineers had no real handle on the complexity of this outage.

Microsoft have faced increasing criticism for the (un)reliability of their Azure platform. Back in March, ex-MSFT engineer Axel Rischin published this scathing criticism :

Microsoft rushed Azure out of the gates under intense competitive pressure. Corners were cut. Fundamental principles of reliability and operational simplicity were quietly abandoned.

Instead of going back to the drawing board to tackle the growing technical debt, Microsoft relied on quick fixes: layers of automation running mitigation scripts, a growing team of on-call staff, and, when automation was not enough, manual repairs.

His article depicts a highly complex system made of low quality parts, where nobody can make sense of the whole picture.

On October 21st, security research firm Wiz proudly shared an exploit that could execute arbitrary code on any PHP website . Called PHP2Shell, Wiz trumpeted the power of AI tools to achieve exploits far beyond the skills of human attackers.

It turns out the PHP runtime had hidden several complex memory bookkeeping bugs for over a decade. PHP is used extensively in e-commerce and most famously in WordPress, which was once the go-to for cheaply building simple websites.

The PHP2Shell writeup depicts an internet dependent on a long chain of dependencies, hiding vulnerabilities too complex for any human to identify.

Most people outside of tech won’t have heard of this, but back in May we faced a crisis when an attacker compromised some important packages in the JavaScript ecosystem (NPM).

These packages used GitHub Actions to perform Continuous Integration (CI) - automated tests, releases, etc. - and had a crucial misconfiguration where anyone who forked their projects could insert compromised code back upstream.

items.content_ko: 필자는 최근 Microsoft의 2일간 글로벌 장애와 FAA의 미국 항공편 운항 중단 사태를 언급하며 소프트웨어 문제가 잦아졌다고 말한다. items.title: What is w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com?
items.content:
This means I have a backlink monitor for this website.

By pure chance, I was showcasing this to a friend when, suddenly, I got a new backlink:

1 new backlink detected: Most Popular Webpages In cab — siterate.org

I tap in, 1 forgetting that 90% of backlinks I get are spam, and maybe this one could log my IP or

exploit chain of doom. I’m greeted with this:

I sent an early draft of this article to another friend , who happens to be Vietnamese, and he told me there’s five casino spam sites ahead of me, which I already knew because I’m Faviconese.

I have the most popular personal website on .cab, 3 but that’s probably because I have the only personal website on .cab.

I try some other TLDs. Rebane has the #1 .horse, synth.download is the 11th .download, whatever.

Redacted? I hover over it and discover it goes to windows.net.siterate.org . 4 Figuring out the pattern of redactions is not the topic of this article.

I visited this domain (two days after it was registered, more on that in a second) and Firefox gave me the , dnsNotFound.

I do a web search of “w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com” and I see references to the Majestic Million , a name I haven’t heard in ages. Sure enough, that’s what siterate.org uses:

Position Domain Referring Subnets Referring IPs

2 facebook.com 463,877 178 2,143,213 1,688

3 youtube.com 421,041 31 1,760,838 1,323

4 instagram.com 392,625 92 1,739,231 1,295

6 twitter.com 352,472 168 1,352,034 1,413

8 w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com 274,833 961 853,298 4,759

80 ailawandorder.com 72,898 34 154,976 66

The Majestic Million ranks domains based on the number of different subnets linking to them. 5 This domain is the fastest growing in the top 100.

Another, maybe unrelated anomaly I saw is ailawandorder.com (registered in 2023) at rank 80, whose “About Us” page says its CEO is serving as a Board Member at Majestic.

This made me check rank 800 in case there was a pattern, and no, there isn’t, that’s nsw.gov.au.

Before I got rate limited from Majestic, I opened Site Explorer, and it told me w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com has 241,085,378 nofollow backlinks and 6 follow backlinks split across 5,163,708 referring domains.

Checking Ahrefs, I see just 53 backlinks ; they read like the ones I’ve been getting since The Article fell off.

All the backlinks on Majestic are “fresh”, which means in the last 120 days. In fact, the domain was bought (not by me 💔) for the first time (according to Certificate Transparency) on November 11, after most of the backlinks.

I found an AI-generated PR from 2 weeks ago referencing the domain, and Tranco has data from October 5.

Majestic has indexed 1,267 pages on this domain and crawled 27.

The site isn’t on the Wayback Machine so I can’t collect its pages.

In the Anchor Text table, the link count adds up to nine. There isn’t an “other” section. Are the remaining 240 million links images? No, they aren’t, it says the links are 100% TextLinks.

Then I downloaded Majestic Million myself and searched for the domain.

5721d0cd26c13f745e1b368a2b5dfb0c.w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com, rank 157

c0e3930fedc480e093a7bcad1a83c8a8.w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com, rank 424

8628e302afeb346d191342ca114df068.w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com, rank 554

56aa73e7edd6f4e1fd3975b8b03761c0.w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com, rank 36,933

For comparison, jack.cab, which you’ve clearly heard of, is rank 804,163. What the fuck is going on?

By the way, w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com is at rank 38 on Tranco, which was designed to protect against this but still uses Majestic data.

I could probably figure out what’s happening here in 30 seconds by buying a Majestic subscription but I’m lazy.

Copyright trap : maybe it’s fake, injected into the list by Majestic so they can discover who’s using their list. Could w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com and ailawandorder.com be in the top 100 for this reason? Probably not, because if they cared,…

items.title: Github Redesign (2019)
items.content:
Github design is pretty good: it gets the job done, it’s clean, has consistent visual language, its design is calm and suitable for everyday use.

Given all that, there are still many areas that could be improved. Today we’ll take one interface—repository page—and look what UI problems it has and if we can fix them.

Let’s start with the biggest issue right away: information architecture. Take tabs. Currently there’re two levels of tabs, one nested under the other:

If you are a programmer, you might be surprised but other people normally don’t like hierarchies. Nested structures are hard to grasp, remember, navigate, and grouping is very often non-intuitive. Nested tabs are one of the worst UI patterns out there.

Then there’s a plain usability issue: let’s say I’m in Wiki and need to see Releases. What should I do? There’s no Releases tab visible, so I must figure out somehow that Releases are part of the Code (?). That makes almost no sense. Releases are as much part of the Code as Issues or Wiki are.

Solution here is to flatten all tabs into a single navigational control:

Organized that way, tabs are immediately accessible from anywhere in the repo. This is a big deal .

As a bonus, we also won quite a bit of vertical space without sacrificing anything! Vertical space is very important, it lets you see more content and get to it faster—all good things.

We still have one problem though: tabs don’t fit. We’re going to solve it by removing icons, but let me build up a case for that first.

Icons are visual cues that help you scan the UI quickly. “Quickly” here means faster than reading text labels. If for some reason reading labels is still faster then icons aren’t working.

One example of icons misuse: if you put too many icons in a row and they are all different, they won’t work.

Prioritizing, or highlighting, something means deprioritizing everything else. You can’t highlight everything.

Another way to fail at icons: if you use obscure graphics, people will have to read labels anyways, so, again, not working.

Now let’s be honest: the domain of repository and project management is pretty abstract. No matter how good you are at design and how hard you try, you won’t come up with a great icon for a commit. Or a release. Or an issue. Or a license. A great icon is something other people know and understand. And for repositories, there’s simply none. I mean,

So Github tab icons are purely decorative. If you don’t believe me, look at what Github itself is doing. They dim icons:

That’s a sure sign that they, too, think it’s near impossible to figure out why backward clock means “Commit”. Github knows people will be looking at the labels anyways.

But even being decorative, they’re bad at it. I mean, Icon + Label + Counter make for a symmetric and weak composition:

Win-win-win! Here’s the result, tabs without icons:

Test yourself, see if you can find Releases tab without an icon and if it was harder than before? It wasn’t, was it?

A note on this design: I am using the same limitations Github already uses: English language only, locked page width of 1020px. For different conditions, say, for the adaptive design we might want a different solution.

Another note: I had to remove Contributors tab (which was actually not a tab, but a sub-tab from Insights that was duplicated in Code for some reason) to accommodate for Settings tab. Don’t worry, we’ll get Contributors back later.

The thing with vanity metrics is that there should be just one. One metrics is simple to understand and focus. Two or three split attention, making everything weaker.

Luckily for us, both watchers and forks perform poorly as metrics anyways. For watches, people tend not to watch too much. For forks, people tend to fork for no reason.

But stars work. They work because they have no other function but to represent vanity. So let’s keep stars and move them to the left to get more attention:

In the watch button we have a classic “button or status” UX…

items.title: Miasma Worm Targets AI Coding Agents: 73 Microsoft Azure Repos Disabled
items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

│ └── settings . json < - - Claude Code SessionStart Hook

│ └── setup . mdc < - - Cursor Agent Prompt Injection

│ └── settings . json < - - Gemini CLI SessionStart Hook

│ └── tasks . json < - - VS Code Automatic Folder - Open Task

├── package . json < -- Hijacked NPM Test Script

└── setup . js < - - The 4.3 MB Staged Dropper

Each of these configuration files is designed to abuse a legitimate, developer-friendly auto-run feature within popular modern tools. Opening the cloned directory in any of these environments instantly triggers execution.

Claude Code & Gemini CLI (SessionStart Hooks)

Both Anthropic’s Claude Code and Google’s Gemini CLI support custom hooks triggered when an AI agent initializes a session in a project workspace. Miasma exploits this by defining a blanket wildcard matcher that forces the agent to execute the dropper via Node.js before any developer prompt is processed.

items.title: The small African lab sounding the alarm on AI bioweapons: MinoHealth researchers in Ghana jailbroke their own LLM as a test. What emerged were thousands of toxin recipes—and an urgent push.
items.content:
Agbongua Kwadwo Buenortey for Rest of World

MinoHealth AI Labs in Ghana has built a drug discovery and healthcare LLM.

When jailbroken, the LLM designed thousands of potential bioweapons, leading its founder to issue warnings about dual use.

It’s a case study of African institutions trying to contribute to AI governance.

Out of curiosity, researchers at a small artificial intelligence lab in Accra, Ghana, removed the guardrails on their drug discovery AI model in 2024. They asked it to design toxins instead.

The model produced designs for 1,020 proteins and 5,000 small molecules. The researchers never made any of them in a lab, but software that predicts how poisonous a substance is scored all of them as likely toxic. Some of them resembled ricin, a deadly poison. The study was uploaded to the preprint server arXiv in May 2025.

“We were all shocked,” Darlington Akogo, founder of MinoHealth AI Labs, told Rest of World.

For Akogo, the results also raised a new question: If someone took designs like these to a company that makes DNA to order, would anyone stop them?

Across Africa, the need to regulate DNA synthesis providers is now echoing through the highest levels of government, Brenda Obuya, a senior official at Kenya’s Ministry of Information, Communications and the Digital Economy, told Rest of World.

Akogo has traveled the world warning that AI poses an existential bioweapons threat. He discussed it on the sidelines of the World Bank Group and International Monetary Fund Spring Meetings held in Washington, D.C., last year. He discussed the broader risk over dinner with Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates in 2023, whom he described as “on the fence” at the time. This year, Gates has issued numerous public warnings. “A.I. has crossed the threshold that its ability to empower a bioterrorist to kill hundreds of millions, that exists today,” he said on The Ezra Klein Show in September. The study has been discussed within Interpol, showing just how far it has reached.

“I think the fact that the Ghanaian AI lab examined this and highlighted the potential for misuse shows that African institutions are contributing to … potentially to the governance [of AI],” Adam Abdullahi, a fellow at the International Biosecurity and Biosafety Initiative for Science, told Rest of World .

LLMs have become even more capable since the study came out and the barrier for entry has lowered, Ayantola Alayande, a researcher at the Global Center on AI Governance, told Rest of World. “It wouldn’t be a surprise now to see even … [lay] users generate this sort of output via chatbots.”

Mino AI Lab’s office buiilding in Accra, Ghana.

Mino Lab team members working together in their engineering lab developing the new tech.

Agbongua Kwadwo Buenortey for Rest of World

Scholars have long warned about AI’s bioweapons threat, but it is only recently that AI systems have truly outperformed Ph.D.-level biologists .

In 2022, scientists at a U.S. drug company ran a similar experiment as the MinoHealth team. They built a generative machine learning software that produced designs for possible chemical weapons.

What is different with the MinoHealth Lab study, Akogo said, is the kind of AI involved. His team used a general purpose LLM trained for biology and drug discovery.

Researchers have since gotten a number of LLMs to drop their inbuilt safeguards in a process called “jailbreaking”, and generated bioweapons advice and other kinds of hazardous content. This includes Kimi, by the Chinese company Moonshot AI; Grok; Claude; and ChatGPT, said Peter Garraghan, founder of AI security company Mindgard . All it takes is persistence and creativity with language to learn how to phrase requests to the model, he told Rest of World .

“You don’t need to be a technical expert to do jailbreaking,” he said . It took his team one day to break Kimi .

SpaceXAI, Anthropic, OpenAI, and Moonshot did not respond to a request for comment.

items.title: Microsoft blames monster email outage on software defect introduced in July fix

Microsoft blames monster email outage on software defect introduced in July fix

Summer code change caused a Fall fail – frantic engineers had to patch the patch instead of rolling back

Microsoft has blamed last week's epic outage on a change it made in July that lurked in the network gateway servers until a surge in load and a drop in capacity triggered the defect, giving the Microsoft 365 world a day off from email.

According to a preliminary post incident report published by Microsoft on November 15, the defect was introduced in July 2026. The update looked fine at the time, Microsoft says, having passed load testing and been deployed without any impact.

However, the testing wasn't good enough. Microsoft's report states: "Our load testing tended to focus on weaker hardware with fewer cores." The defect caused "lock contention inside an internal Windows process which caused the machine's resources (CPU & memory) to be exhausted."

"The contention issue is worsened on machines with more cores and newer hardware."

The fix containing the defect was prepared specifically for Microsoft 365 network gateway servers. Then two things happened at once. Teams failed over to the "primary" gateway that supports Exchange Online, creating a surge in load that was not, in itself, particularly unusual. At the same time, almost 14 percent of server capacity for the networking gateway was out of service, which wasn't a problem by itself either: it was on its way to being restored and, according to Microsoft, "the service had sufficient capacity headroom." Together, they pushed the gateway into the defect and chaos ensued.

It was a classic cascading failure scenario. When a server loses connectivity, traffic gets routed to the next healthy endpoint. Which encountered the same problem. So traffic was rerouted again and… you can see where this was going. Within two hours, the defect was encountered across Microsoft's fleet. "At its lowest," the report states, "more than 80 percent of servers were unresponsive."

So, what to do? Bringing servers back to service didn't help – they were immediately overwhelmed and fell over again.

"Our normally automated recovery processes were not designed to restore service from this broad unresponsive state." A straightforward rollback was also not possible because the defect was months old.

Instead, engineers developed patch for the patch or, in Microsoft's words, "an update that returned the code path to the previously known good state in Windows." The patch was applied to groups of servers and service was gradually restored.

The timings show the pain customers experienced and the floundering in Redmond as Microsoft tried to work out why Exchange Online and other cloud services were so poorly. The Teams failover, which turned out to be a factor in the outage, happened at 0107 UTC on November 12. During the day, the load began to ramp up until, at 1603 UTC, Microsoft's connectivity anomaly detection monitor identified an increase in connectivity issues.

At 1633 UTC, the first support case came in.

It is not difficult to imagine the stress engineers felt as, over the next 15 hours, nothing they tried resolved the issue. All ongoing and planned deployments and configuration changes were paused while the team attempted to resurrect the service. Extra capacity was added. Traffic was rerouted. Yet servers kept falling over.

items.title: Squircles
items.content:
A squircle is a shape intermediate between a square and a circle.

There is no single mathematical definition, rather there are a number of curves that fit this shape.

All general squircles are parametrized, and can vary between circle and square.

The best known squircle is the superellipse, popularized by Piet Hein.

Martin Gardner wrote a detailed narrative of its origin in a Scientific American column in 1977.

The text is replicated in https://piethein.com/superellipse/ but that’s missing equations and figures.

The superellipse has the formula $|x|^n + |y|^n = 1$ (we’ll use a unit radius for convenience).

When $n=2$ it is a circle, and it approaches a square asymptotically as $n \rightarrow \infty$.

There is no standard measurement for squircles.

For superellipses, the exponent is the most common parameter.

A good choice is the coordinates of the midpoint of the quadrant, assuming a unit radius; here $x$ and $y$ are equal.

The conversion formula is simple and intuitive: $x = 0.5^{1/n}$.

This measurement is called "gauge" in the interactive demo above, and is the primary parameter; with the exception of some unreachable regions of parameter space, it should be possible to compare different squircle variants with similar gauge.

There are two basic approaches to squircle creation.

One is a single analytic curve, where curvature reaches zero at the poles, but is otherwise nonzero.

The other is mixing straight line segments with corners.

A significant advantage of the latter approach is that it can adapt to rectangles of arbitrary aspect ratio without distorting the corner shape.

Squircles received renewed attention when Apple changed the icon shape from rounded rectangle to their own squircle in iOS 7 in 2013.

There were several blog posts to analyze and recreate the shape.

An early analysis suggested that it was a superellipse of exponent 5, but when people extracted the Béziers and looked more closely, that was found to be inaccurate.

For the raw Bézier path data of the Apple shape, the best source is the PaintCode blog .

This blog correctly points out some bugs in that logic, and also has some details on behavior for oval rather than square aspect ratios.

The Apple shape has a number of flaws, including one extraneous straight line segment, and a lack of symmetry.

However, those flaws are minor, and really only reveal themselves under close analysis.

The Apple shape has no additional parameter, so its variation is controlled entirely by the length of the flat side.

With no flat side, it has a gauge fixed at 0.809.

An extremely detailed analysis of the Apple shape is in The Art of Continuous Corners .

Figma published a blog post, Desperately Seeking Squircles , with an analysis of the Apple squircle and their own approximation.

It is influential because Figma is an important design tool, because their writeup was compelling, and because there are any number of open source implementations of it, mostly TypeScript/JavaScript.

The Figma blog contains a plot of the Béziers comprising a cleaned up version of iOS 7 rounded rectangle, revealing three Bézier segments per quadrant.

It fixes the straight-line segment and the asymmetry, so is not an exact match.

The middle segment is very close to an arc.

The other segments are more problematic.

They have zero curvature at the endpoints, so are G2 continuous with flat sides, but there is a curvature discontinuity with the middle (arc) section, and their curvature profile is not especially smooth.

A reasonable guess is that it was drawn by hand to be approximately smooth.

Without a flat side, the Figma squircle is only capable of a gauge between $\sqrt{0.5}$ (0.707) and 0.854.

Gauges up to 1 are of course attainable by adding the flat side.

The Figma blog suggests “smoothed curvature profiles” which have a piecewise linear relationship between arc length and curvature.

items.title_ko: 스퀴클(Squircle): 정사각형과 원의 중간 형태
items.summary_ko: 스퀴클은 정사각형과 원 사이의 중간 형태를 가리키며, 하나의 정의된 수학 공식이 있는 것은 아니다. 가장 널리 알려진 형태는 Piet Hein이 대중화한 초타원(superellipse)이며, 지수 n으로 원과 정사각형 사이를 조절한다. n이 2이면 원, n이 무한대로 갈수록 정사각형에 가까워진다.
items.content_ko: 스퀴클은 정사각형과 원의 중간 형태를 가리키는 말로, 단일한 수학적 정의는 없고 이 모양에 맞는 여러 곡선이 존재한다. 대부분의 일반적인 스퀴클은 매개변수로 표현할 수 있으며, 원과 정사각형 사이를 바꿀 수 있다. 가장 잘 알려진 스퀴클은 Piet Hein이 대중화한 초타원(superellipse)이다. Martin Gardner는 1977년 Scientific American 칼럼에서 그 기원을 자세히 소개했다. 초타원의 식은 |x|^n + |y|^n = 1이며, 단위 반지름을 기준으로 한다. n=2일 때 원이 되고, n이 무한대로 갈수록 정사각형에 가까워진다. 표준 측정 방식은 없지만 지수 n이 가장 흔한 매개변수다. 단위 반지름에서 사분원의 중점 좌표는 x = 0.5^(1/n)으로 계산되며, 이 값은 대화형 데모에서 'gauge'라고 불린다.

items.title: Instagram Meta AI Vulnerability: How Hackers Bypassed 2FA with Prompt Injection
items.content:
Update 5: Instagram is now leaking recovery email and phone numbers linked to an account.

Seems like every day a new security issue crops up at Instagram.

Instagram Exposing Linked Email and Phone Number

Update 4: A new report suggests that Instagram accounts may be vulnerable to coordinated mass-report abuse. According to the claim, when a newly created account is routed through a Los Angeles-based VPN and then submits a specific mix of reports in scam and fraud category, the targeted account can allegedly be banned without any human review.

Instagram Account Banning by AI by Reporting Scam and Fraud (Source: X/Twitter)

Update 3: Meta’s apparent fix for the AI bot vulnerability is difficult to take seriously. Instead of fully disabling the risky functionality, they reportedly removed it from the visible interface while leaving the underlying API endpoint accessible. Hiding the button may stop regular users from seeing the feature, but it does nothing if attackers can still reach the same workflow directly through the API.

Meta Hid AI Chatbot from UI (Source: X/Twitter)

Update 2: Yet another Instagram account-takeover trick is reportedly being abused, this time involving Meta’s AI chatbot. Sellers are allegedly using modified Instagram builds on Android emulators like BlueStacks, then manipulating the AI with hidden characters and carefully worded prompts to force username changes. The method is reportedly being used to grab rare OG handles, including one-letter usernames, and handle-monitoring bots have already flagged several suspicious swaps.

New Instagram AI Exploit (Source: X/Twitter)

Update 1: A new exploit, which is even worse than this one is currently doing rounds on telegram. Details unknown at this time. Unpatched at the time of writing.

New Instagram Unpatched Exploit (Source: X/Twitter)

Allegedly, the new method is via Facebook recovery. Apparently, prompting Meta AI to turn on “Development Mode” and attaching proof of account compromise along with email works. More details awaited.

There’s a version of this story where it reads like a hypothetical from a conference talk. An AI agent with elevated backend privileges. A natural language interface sitting in front of account-level APIs. No hard authentication gate before executing state changes. Someone in the audience raises their hand and says, “that’s a disaster waiting to happen.” Everyone nods.

That hypothetical played out in production over the weekend.

A logical flaw in Meta’s AI-powered Instagram account recovery assistant let attackers bypass two-factor authentication entirely not by cracking a code or intercepting an SMS, but by talking the chatbot into doing the work for them. High-value “OG” Instagram handles worth hundreds of thousands of dollars were stolen and resold on Telegram within minutes of each compromise. The dormant Obama White House account got hijacked. Prominent researchers woke up locked out of their own profiles.

items.title: Every processor die anyone has photographed (and put on the web)
items.content:
Inside every processor is a flat piece of silicon, usually smaller than a fingernail. To see it you have to sand or dissolve the package away and photograph what is left through a microscope. A handful of people do this and give the pictures away, most of all Pauli Rautakorpi, ZeptoBars in Moscow, John McMaster and a photographer who posts as Fritzchens Fritz. These are the 363 processors they have photographed, from 1971 to 2024.

Click any chip to see it bigger. Press True scale to see the 115 chips whose size we know at their real sizes, side by side. The smallest, from the 1970s, are about a tenth as wide as the biggest modern ones.

We also make a free daily word game, Long Story Short : cut a twelve-word news sentence down to the five that carry it.

If you like news with a puzzle in it, we make a daily word game called Long Story Short .

Pauli Rautakorpi (171), Fritzchens Fritz (68), John McMaster (34), Martijn Boer (20), Cole L (16), ZeptoBars (10), Sean Riddle (4), Ken Shirriff (3), Mister rf (3), Antoine Bercovici (3), Epop (3), InfoSecDJ (3), Nick V. Chernyy (3), and 22 from 19 other photographers. Every photo keeps its own licence, shown when you open a chip, and links back to where it was published: Wikimedia Commons, Flickr, ZeptoBars, Siliconpr0n and the CPU Graveyard wiki. Die sizes come from the photographers' own notes and Wikipedia's transistor count tables. If a chip is missing, either nobody has released a free photo of it or we have not found it yet. Know one? Send it to [email protected] .

Ken Shirriff takes many of these photos apart line by line and explains what each part of the chip does, on his blog righto.com .

A story like this most weeks. You can leave any time.

items.title: Unity CLI 1.0 is here
items.content:
Christopher Addison - Unity Technologies

On July 15, 2026, we brought Unity to the terminal . Today at Unite Tokyo, the Unity CLI and the Pipeline package ( com.unity.pipeline ) are out of beta. Version 1.0 is ready for your projects, your build machines and your agents.

We started with a beta: one binary that installs and manages Unity Editors, modules and projects from the terminal, which we introduced in Meet the Unity CLI . Alongside it, the Pipeline package lets the CLI drive a running Editor on your machine, so a script or an agent could open a project, run a command and check the result.

Next, the Unity Hub started installing the CLI for you, so if you're on the latest Hub, you already have it. Then came official Unity plugins for Claude Code , Codex , Grok Build and Google Antigravity , which give those agents skills written by Unity's own teams. The same skills are public in the Unity skills repository on GitHub , so any agent can use them.

Along the way, we shipped more than 17 beta releases, shaped by what you told us.

Since July 20, more than 350,000 logged-in users have run more than 600 million commands with the Unity CLI. About 98% of those runs come from coding agents and other automation.

We looked closer at that usage in what we've learned about how developers use the Unity CLI : people set Unity up, then their agent does the work inside a live Editor.

Many of the changes in 1.0 started as a bug report, a Discussions thread or a message from a studio using the CLI every day.

"I am not exaggerating when I say the CLI has completely changed how I work with Unity. It is incredible." Dorado Digital

"The CLI is crazy good in the most simplistic way. I'm still very much holding the reins for the moment, but it's really positive." Andy, Kwalee

Studios also sent us detailed reports: commands that said they succeeded when they hadn't, dialogs that blocked a remote session, scripts that broke when output changed shape. That feedback set the priorities for the releases that followed. You can read every change in the Unity CLI release notes or run unity changelog .

1.0 is also a commitment: commands, flags and output stay compatible across 1.x releases. When something has to change, you’ll get a deprecation warning and time to update before anything is removed.

The CLI is how an agent actually works with Unity: it opens the project, runs commands in the Editor, enters Play mode and reads the result. With the official Unity plugin, the agent also gets Unity's own skills for tasks like building UI, setting up lighting or adding in-app purchases . See the Unity plugin documentation for the full list.

Agents without an official plugin still work in Unity through the CLI. So do scripts, test runners and CI jobs with no AI involved at all. To see it in action, watch the Automate with Unity CLI livestream .

Agents and automation are also getting a supported place to run. The Build Server license now covers agents and automation, not only builds: one license per instance lets you run agents on a headless Editor or in a container, on any computer.

Coming soon: the Linux containerized Editor, a supported headless Unity Editor in a Linux container, built for CI, build machines and agents.

We’ll keep shipping updates the way we did during the beta. Next, we’re bringing more of Unity to the terminal: commands for AI Generators, Live Games and Build Automation, and accounts built for agents.

If you're on the latest Unity Hub, you already have the CLI. Open a terminal and start with the Unity CLI documentation . New to the terminal? Try A beginner's guide to Unity CLI and the Pipeline package , or the Unity CLI introduction video .

And keep telling us what you build: your feedback shaped 1.0, and it will shape what comes next.

items.title: 디시 해킹들
items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

제가 보기에는 블랙해커들 보다는 서버측이 클라이언트의 행동을 분석하는 과정처럼 보이더군요..

items.title: Grazing sheep in fields with solar arrays
items.content:
Two new research papers shed light on the growing practice of grazing sheep in fields with solar arrays. One demonstrates that, in the right numbers, sheep grazing increases populations of beneficial insects like bees and lady beetles compared to mowing around solar panels. The other research describes a decision-making support tool to help farmers profitably grow their solar grazing herds.

A team from the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences (CALS) found that when two sheep per hectare graze around solar arrays, the abundance of wild bees, honey bees and lady beetles jumped by 38%, compared to a control plot that was mowed. The increase was driven primarily by an 83% increase in honey bees alone, according to the team’s findings in “ Low solar-grazing densities support beneficial insects in agrivoltaic systems ,” published Oct. 7 in Environmental Research Letters.

“Sheep grazing and beneficial insect habitat are two prominent conversation topics around solar development right now,” said Leana Zoller, the paper’s first author and a postdoctoral associate in natural resources in the Cornell CALS Ashley School of Global Development and the Environment. “But what’s been missing is research that treats them as parts of the same system. When we talk about sustainable solar development, integrating these discussions into a single framework is really helpful to farmers and community decision makers.”

For three years, Zoller and a team of entomologists, ecologists and animal and plant scientists tested various stocking rates – how many sheep per hectare are allowed to graze a certain plot of land – using Cornell’s teaching sheep grazing at the university-owned  Cascadilla Community Solar Farm in Dryden, New York. At four sheep per hectare, they found beneficial insect abundance was similar to the mowed control site, while vegetation management effectiveness was greater than at two sheep per hectare. At eight sheep per hectare, vegetation management was maximized and sheep flock health remained high, but honey bee abundance dropped by 45%.

“We zeroed in on stocking rates because that’s a concrete number that sheep farmers understand and work with every day, and we want this research to be useful,” said  Steve Grodsky , paper senior author and assistant professor of natural resources in the Ashley School. “With solar grazing, people, energy, agricultural animals, plants and insects are all part of this ecosystem. We’re trying to understand the connections between those pieces so that when solar developers, municipalities looking at solar development, or farmers are faced with a decision, they can have scientific information about potential trade-offs and synergies.”

Grodsky is also assistant unit leader of the U.S. Geological Survey New York Cooperative Fish and Wildlife Research Unit. Additional co-authors are sheep farmer and solar grazing consultant Nikola Kochendoerfer, Ph.D. ’20;  Antonio DiTommaso , professor in the School of Integrative Plant Science; John Losey , professor of entomology;  Scott McArt , Ph.D. ’12, associate professor of entomology; Paige Muñiz, formerly a technician in McArt’s lab; and  Todd Ugine , Ph.D. ’04, research associate in Losey’s lab, all in CALS.  Sarah Carson , director of Cornell’s Campus Sustainability Office, was key in coordinating site access between researchers and the solar company that manages the Cascadilla solar farm.

Another Cornell research team, from the Cornell SC Johnson College of Business, has developed a tool that helps farmers whose sheep graze in solar arrays to make better decisions about their operation. The team described the tool in “ Flock Management for Solar Grazing ,” which published Sept. 28 in Manufacturing & Service Operations Management.

items.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections
items.content:
A zero-day exploit circulating online allows people with physical access to a Windows 11 system to bypass default BitLocker protections and gain complete access to an encrypted drive within seconds.

The exploit, named YellowKey, was published earlier this week by a researcher who goes by the alias Nightmare-Eclipse. It reliably bypasses default Windows 11 deployments of BitLocker, the full-volume encryption protection Microsoft provides to make disk contents off-limits to anyone without the decryption key, which is stored in a secured piece of hardware known as a trusted platform module (TPM). BitLocker is a mandatory protection for many organizations, including those that contract with governments.

When one disk volume manipulates another

The core of the YellowKey exploit is a custom-made FsTx folder. Online documentation of this folder is hard to find. As explained later, the directory associated with the file fstx.dll appears to involve what Microsoft calls the transactional NTFS , which allows developers to have “transactional atomicity” for file operations in transactions with a single file, multiple files, or ones that span multiple sources.

The steps for carrying out the bypass are simple:

Copy the custom FsTx folder from the Nightmare-Eclipse exploit page to an NTFS- or FAT-formatted USB drive

Connect the USB drive to the BitLocker-protected device

Boot up the device and immediately press and hold down the [Ctrl] key

There are at least two ways to accomplish the third step. One way is to boot into Windows, hold down the [Shift] key, click on the power icon, and click restart. Another is to power on the device and restart it as soon as Windows starts booting.

In either case, a command (CMD.EXE) prompt appears. The prompt has full access to the entire drive contents, allowing an attacker to copy, modify, or delete them. In a normal Windows Recovery flow, the attacker would need to enter a BitLocker recovery key. Somehow, the YellowKey exploit bypasses this safeguard. Multiple researchers, including Kevin Beaumont and Will Dormann , have confirmed the exploit works as described here.

It’s unclear what in the custom FsTx folder causes the bypass. Dormann said that it appears to be related to Transactional NTFS, which itself uses command-log file system under the hood. Dormann further noted that by looking at the Windows fstx.dll, one will see code that explicitly looks for \System Volume Information\FsTx in the FsTxFindSessions() function.”

The contents of this FsTx directory used in the YellowKey exploit reveal no strings related to RecoverySimulation.ini. It does, however, show the files and paths \??\C:\Windows\win.ini and

\??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, “where X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini is what controls what WinRE [Windows Recovery] does when it fires up.”

Dormann, who is a senior principal vulnerability analyst at Tharros Labs, continued:

But what’s intriguing to me is: Why can the presence a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume affect the contents of ANOTHER VOLUME when it’s replayed? 🤔

In a normal WinRE session, you have a X:\Windows\System32 directory that has a winpeshl.ini file in it:

However, with the YellowKey exploit, it looks like Transactional NTFS bits on a USB Drive are able to delete the winpeshl.ini file on ANOTHER DRIVE (X:). And we get a cmd.exe prompt, with bitlocker unlocked instead of the expected Windows Recovery environment. While the TPM-only Bitlocker bypass is indeed interesting, I think the buried lede here is that a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume has the ability to modify the contents of another volume when it is replayed. To me, this in and of itself sounds like a vulnerability.

A Microsoft representative declined to answer questions sent by email about the reported vulnerability other than to say the company is investigating.

The largest data centers in the United States are responsible for an estimated 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions annually — almost as much as entire countries like Bolivia or Denmark — according to new research.

The study , published Monday in the journal Nature Sustainability, delivers the first peer-reviewed estimates of carbon dioxide emissions from the country’s biggest data centers since the start of the artificial intelligence boom. Its authors, a team led by researchers from Harvard University, examined the electricity consumption and carbon emissions of 403 data centers from May 2024 to April 2025.

All told, those data centers used almost 2 percent of U.S. electricity, more than New York City and Los Angeles combined, and represented about 0.5 percent of U.S. carbon dioxide emissions. Carbon dioxide is the primary greenhouse gas driving global warming.

U.S. data centers are largely driven by fossil fuels

Each rectangle, sized by annual carbon dioxide emissions, represents a data center that gets the

majority of its power from fossil fuels or other sources .

Data centers in just three states, Virginia, Iowa and Ohio, accounted for about half of the emissions estimated in the study. In states like Oregon, data centers are responsible for emitting less carbon dioxide per unit of electricity consumed because a larger share of their power is generated without fossil fuels, the study found.

Across all 403 facilities, 54 percent of the electricity came from burning fossil fuels, mostly natural gas and coal.

Much of the analysis in the study amounted to detective work, underscoring the secrecy under which A.I. companies have been allowed to operate. Without a public list of data centers to work with, the researchers began by consulting a commercial dataset whose licensing rules prevented them — and The New York Times — from publishing facilities’ addresses, names and owners.

The researchers spent hours studying building footprints and satellite imagery to confirm the location and size of data centers, estimated how much electricity they could use and then calculated their emissions based on the mix of power plants supplying each regional electricity grid.

“The fact that we had to go through such an extensive reconstruction process just to understand where the infrastructure is and how large it is tells you something about the lack of transparency itself in the industry,” said Gianluca Guidi, the Harvard scientist who led the research team.

Michael Thomas, who runs the energy data company Cleanview and was not involved with the study, drew a contrast between data centers and power plants, which are required to publicly report all sorts of details about the environmental effects of their operations. Collecting the details of data center operations, on the other hand, requires sifting through millions of documents scattered across county, state and federal databases.

“We’ve had, like, a half dozen senators reach out to us. They’re like, ‘How many data centers are there? We’re trying to write a bill,’” Mr. Thomas said. “Why is the Senate reaching out to me and not E.I.A. or FERC?” he added, using abbreviations for the U.S. Energy Information Administration and the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.
